> 此法门中，坐禅元不看心，亦不看净，亦不是不动。

Three ways of sitting that look like practice, and the chapter takes them apart one at a time.

## 看心: watching a phantom with a phantom

*If you say "watch the mind" — the mind is originally delusion; delusion is like an illusion, so there is nothing to watch.*

The argument is not that the mind is too subtle to observe. It is that the act of watching manufactures a second instance of the problem. The mind is a dependent arising, an image produced by conditions; to set up a watcher over it is to add a watcher-image and a watched-image, both of the same kind. One illusion inspecting another illusion and calling the result insight.

Anyone who has tried it knows the texture: you sit, you notice you are thinking, you feel pleased at having noticed, and then you notice the pleasure. The chain does not end. Each link is a new object for the previous link.

## 看净: building the very thing you want to be rid of

*If you say "watch purity" — human nature is originally pure; because of deluded thoughts the true suchness is covered. Apart from deluded thoughts, the nature is pure. Not seeing that the nature is originally pure, you give rise to a mind that watches purity, and so produce the delusion of purity. Purity has no mark, yet you establish purity as a mark; the knowing one has no location, so this is delusion. Purity being markless, you nonetheless set up a mark of purity — this view obstructs its own root.*

The structure of the mistake is stated exactly: purity has no mark, and the practice consists in manufacturing a mark for it. What you then experience is the mark, not the purity. And because the mark is maintained by effort, its maintenance becomes the practice, and the effort is mistaken for attainment.

The commentary puts the same point in its own vocabulary: this is a *construction* — a boundary drawn between clean and dirty, then defended. The nature's purity is not a boundary; it is the absence of one.

## 不动: a body that sits still while the mouth runs

*If you cultivate immobility — when you see anyone, not seeing their right and wrong, good and bad, faults, that is the immobility of self-nature. Deluded people may have a body that does not move, but open their mouths and speak of others' right and wrong, long and short, likes and dislikes; this is contrary to the way.*

This is the funniest and least comfortable of the three. The test of stillness is not posture but speech. A person can hold a posture for an hour and spend the following ten minutes ranking colleagues, and the posture has done nothing except provide a good story about the morning.

## The redefinition

Then the definition, which is the chapter's whole content:

*What is called sitting meditation? In this dharma-gate, without obstruction, outside all good and evil states the mind does not arise — this is called sitting. Inside, seeing the self-nature unmoved — this is called chan.*

*Outside, leaving marks is chan; inside, not being disordered is concentration. If outside you cling to marks, the mind inside is disordered. If outside you leave marks, the mind is not disordered. The nature is originally pure and still; only because you see states and think about states does it become disordered. If seeing all states the mind is not disordered, that is true concentration.*

Sitting becomes an activity of not being dragged. Chan becomes an activity of not being captured by a mark. Neither has a location. Both can be done while walking to a meeting.

## 不见 is not blindness

The phrase *not seeing others' faults* needs a guard against its counterfeit. It does not mean refusing to notice that a colleague is incompetent, or that a plan is wrong. It means not installing a verdict and a rank on the basis of the noticing.

The commentary frames the difference as follows: a judgment is a boundary drawn and then treated as part of the object; the nature's immobility is a whole that does not need the boundary in order to hold what is in front of it. You can see the error clearly and not file the person under it. Most of us cannot, and the filing is what keeps the seat warm.

## The test

In your next meeting, count the judgments you form about someone's competence. Do not try to stop forming them. Just count. Then notice what each judgment did to your body — a small tightening, a slight leaning back.

The count is the practice. The tightening is the evidence that the judgment was not free.
